title: Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (100/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Norton
items.stem: Which of the following is not among the University Wits ?
items.explanation: Thomas Norton (co-author of Gorboduc with Thomas Sackville) was an Elizabethan lawyer and parliamentarian, not one of the University Wits. The University Wits included Cambridge and Oxford graduates like John Lyly, Thomas Nashe, George Peele, Robert Greene, Thomas Lodge, and Christopher Marlowe.

items.title: Q2 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem: Which of the following was not an Irish playwright ?
items.explanation: Harold Pinter was an English playwright born in Hackney, London, best known for his 'comedies of menace' like The Birthday Party. George Bernard Shaw, J. M. Synge, and Oscar Wilde were all Irish-born dramatists.

items.title: Q3 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit I: Drama · Adolphus William Ward
items.stem: Who wrote the famous book History of Dramatic English Literature ?
items.explanation: Adolphus William Ward wrote the landmark scholarly study A History of English Dramatic Literature to the Death of Queen Anne (first published in two volumes in 1875). It remains a foundational Victorian history of early English drama.

items.title: Q4 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Medieval Period · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: The plays which are based on the Biblical stories are known as
items.explanation: Medieval Mystery plays dramatized biblical narratives from the Creation to the Last Judgment and were performed by trade guilds (craft 'mysteries'). Miracle plays depicted the lives and miracles of saints, while Morality plays used allegorical characters to teach moral lessons.

items.title: Q5 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit VI: English in India · Kalidasa
items.stem: Who is the author of Abhijanasakuntalam ?
items.explanation: Kalidasa authored Abhijnanasakuntalam (The Recognition of Shakuntala), the celebrated classical Sanskrit nataka (drama) adapting the story of Dushyanta and Shakuntala from the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata.

items.title: Q6 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit II: Poetry · John Masefield
items.stem: Which of the following is not known as a 'War Poet' in English Literature ?
items.explanation: Rupert Brooke, Siegfried Sassoon, and Wilfred Owen are canonical First World War ('Trench') poets. John Masefield (misspelled 'John Maxfield' in the paper) was Britain's Poet Laureate known primarily for maritime poems like 'Sea-Fever' rather than as a War Poet.

items.title: Q7 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: The line "That is no country for old men" figures in which of the following poems ?
options: The Death of the Hired Man
items.explanation: 'That is no country for old men' is the famous opening line of W. B. Yeats's poem 'Sailing to Byzantium' (published in The Tower, 1928), which contrasts the transient world of youth and sensual nature with the timeless permanence of art.

items.title: Q8 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: American Renaissance & Realism (19th C) · Unit II: Poetry · Emily Dickinson
items.stem: The line "Because I could not stop for Death-He kindly stopped for me" figures in whose poetry ?
items.explanation: 'Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –' opens one of American poet Emily Dickinson's best-known lyrics (Poem 479 / 712), personifying Death as a courteous gentleman suitor in a carriage.

items.title: Q9 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem: Lycidas is an example of which of the following ?
items.explanation: John Milton's Lycidas (1637), written to commemorate his Cambridge classmate Edward King who drowned in the Irish Sea, is a classical pastoral elegy (listed here as 'Pastoral epic' ) employing the convention of shepherds mourning a fellow swain.

items.title: Q10 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem: Robert Browning's "My Last Duchess" is an example of
items.explanation: Robert Browning's 'My Last Duchess' (published in Dramatic Lyrics, 1842) is the quintessential Victorian dramatic monologue, in which the Duke of Ferrara addresses a silent envoy while unwittingly revealing his own arrogance and cruelty.

items.title: Q11 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Henry Fielding
items.stem: Which of the following was not a modernist writer ?
items.explanation: Henry Fielding (1707–1754) was an eighteenth-century Augustan novelist and dramatist known for Joseph Andrews and Tom Jones, whereas James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, and D. H. Lawrence were major twentieth-century modernist novelists.

items.title: Q12 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Gabriel Garcia Marquez
items.stem: Gabriel Garcia Marquez is famous for which of the following ?
items.explanation: Colombian Nobel laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez is a master of Magic Realism, seamlessly blending fantastical and mythic elements into realistic historical settings in novels such as One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967).

items.title: Q13 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Albert Camus
items.stem: Who has written The Myth of Sisyphus ?
items.explanation: Albert Camus wrote the philosophical essay The Myth of Sisyphus (Le Mythe de Sisyphe, 1942), using the Greek myth of Sisyphus eternally rolling a boulder uphill to illustrate the philosophy of the absurd.

items.title: Q14 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Patrick White
items.stem: In Patrick White's Voss, the character Voss is :
options: a crazy German trying to make his experience worthwhile
items.explanation: In Patrick White's novel Voss (1957), the German expedition leader Johann Ulrich Voss undertakes a journey across the Australian interior that serves primarily as a metaphysical and spiritual quest exploring his inner self and hubris.

items.title: Q15 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Nadine Gordimer
items.stem: Nadine Gordimer is a :
items.explanation: Nadine Gordimer (1923-2014), Nobel laureate, was a white South African novelist writing against apartheid. She was not Nigerian or Kenyan.

items.title: Q16 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle
items.stem: Who is the author of French Revolution ?
items.explanation: Thomas Carlyle authored The French Revolution: A History (1837), a three-volume historical work celebrated for its dramatic, prophetic prose style and vivid characterization of revolutionary upheaval.

items.title: Q17 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: Who has written The Metaphysical Poets ?
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot wrote the influential critical essay 'The Metaphysical Poets' (1921) as a review of Herbert Grierson's anthology Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century, introducing the concept of 'dissociation of sensibility'.

items.title: Q18 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Renaissance · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More
items.stem: Who wrote the famous text Dignity of Man ?
items.explanation: Renaissance humanist Sir Thomas More translated the biography and writings of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (author of the Oration on the Dignity of Man) into English in 1510, making Thomas More the credited answer among the given Tudor writers.

items.title: Q19 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The line "Drop, drop, slow tears" is the example of :
items.explanation: Phineas Fletcher's famous devotional line 'Drop, drop, slow tears' uses consecutive heavy stresses ('Drop, drop' and 'slow tears'), making it a classic textbook example of the spondee (a metrical foot of two stressed syllables).

items.title: Q20 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following is not correct about "Cognitive approach to language learning" ?
options: It lays emphasis on conscious acquisition of language
It seeks intellectual understanding by the learner
It seeks a reasonable understanding of structure of the language to develop better use of language
It rejects the teaching of grammar and language rules
items.explanation: The cognitive approach to language learning emphasizes conscious rule acquisition, mental processing, and an intellectual grasp of grammatical structures; therefore, the claim that it rejects the teaching of grammar and language rules is incorrect.

items.title: Q21 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Ferdinand de Saussure
items.stem: Who is the author of A Course in General Linguistics ?
items.explanation: Course in General Linguistics (Cours de linguistique generale, 1916) was compiled by Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye from Ferdinand de Saussure's lecture notes at the University of Geneva, laying the foundation for modern structural linguistics.

items.title: Q22 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Of the following, what is not true about Pidgins and Creoles ?
options: Spoken by the Third World Countries
New languages in their own right
Developed during the periods of linguistic crisis
items.explanation: Modern sociolinguistics recognizes pidgins and creoles as rule-governed contact languages in their own right rather than 'distorted' or 'corrupt' versions of standard languages, making statement (2) false.

items.title: Q23 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Raja Ram Mohan Roy
items.stem: Who wrote "A Defence of Hindoo Theism" ?
items.explanation: Social reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy published A Defence of Hindoo Theism in 1817 to vindicate monotheistic Vedantic philosophy against orthodox idol-worship arguments.

items.title: Q24 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Who is the author of French novel, Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers ?
items.explanation: Nineteenth-century Indian poet Toru Dutt wrote Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers (published posthumously in Paris in 1879), making it the first novel in French by an Indian writer.

items.title: Q25 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Arun Kolatkar
items.stem: Who has written Jejuri ?
items.explanation: Arun Kolatkar wrote Jejuri (1976), a Commonwealth Writers' Prize-winning sequence of 31 modernist poems chronicling a skeptical visitor's pilgrimage to the temple town of Khandoba in Maharashtra.

items.title: Q26 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: Which of the following is considered as the first published composition in English by an Indian ?
items.explanation: Cavelly Venkata Boriah's 'Account of the Jains' (written in 1803 and published in Asiatic Researches in 1809) is regarded by literary historians such as M. K. Naik as the first published composition in English by an Indian.

items.title: Q27 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Khushwant Singh
items.stem: Who is the author of Mano Majra ?
items.explanation: Khushwant Singh's classic Partition novel Train to Pakistan (1956) was originally titled and published in the United States as Mano Majra, named after the fictional border village where the novel is set.

items.title: Q28 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Arvind Krishna Mehrotra
items.stem: Which of the following poets describes himself as "not an Indian poet but a poet writing a universal language of poetry, of feeling, of love and hate and sex" ?
items.explanation: Arvind Krishna Mehrotra described himself as 'not an Indian poet but a poet writing a universal language of poetry, of feeling, of love and hate and sex,' rejecting narrow nationalist labels for Indian English verse.

items.title: Q29 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Which of the following periods in African American writing is called "Harlem Renaissance" ?
items.explanation: The Harlem Renaissance is the flowering of African American art and writing that began in the late 1910s and ran through the 1920s-30s. Among these options, 1917-1920 marks its start; the others fit other movements. (Key doubtful: option set is loose.)

items.title: Q30 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Michel Foucault
items.stem: Who introduced the concept of "Biopower" ?
items.explanation: French philosopher Michel Foucault introduced the concept of 'biopower' (biopouvoir) in his Collège de France lectures and The History of Sexuality, Vol. 1 (1976) to describe how modern states regulate human populations through biological and disciplinary control.

items.title: Q31 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Burns
items.stem: "These English songs gravel one to death". This statement is attributed to
items.explanation: Scottish poet Robert Burns remarked in a September 1794 letter to George Thomson, 'These English songs gravel me to death,' explaining that writing lyrics in standard English rather than his native Scots dialect felt unnatural to him.

items.title: Q32 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
Who made this following statement ?
"Truly neither philosopher nor historiographer could have entered into the gates of popular judgements, if they had not taken a great passport of poetry".
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney made this statement in the opening movement of An Apology for Poetry (1595), arguing that poetry was the earliest cradle of learning through which ancient philosophers and historians gained popular reception.

items.title: Q33 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Salman Rushdie
items.stem: Midnight's Children is a representative text of :
items.explanation: Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981) is a canonical text of Postmodernism (specifically historiographic metafiction), using magic realism, fragmented self-reflexive narration, and unreliable memory to interrogate national history.

items.title: Q34 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: "The Frontiers of Criticism" by T. S. Eliot is associated with :
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot's 1956 lecture 'The Frontiers of Criticism' (collected in On Poetry and Poets, 1957) reflects on the rise of close reading and what he famously termed 'lemon-squeezer' criticism, directly engaging with New Criticism.

items.title: Q35 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Who defined criticism as "disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world" ?
items.explanation: Matthew Arnold defined criticism as 'a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world' in his landmark essay 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time' (1864).

items.title: Q36 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: According to Edward Albert, the years 1550-1630 is known as :
items.explanation: In A History of English Literature (1923), literary historian Edward Albert classifies the period from 1550 to 1630 as 'The Age of Elizabeth,' encompassing the flowering of Renaissance poetry and Jacobean drama.

items.title: Q37 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Emily Bronte
items.stem: Which of the following is not a Feminist Critic ?
items.explanation: Emily Bronte (1818–1848) was a Victorian novelist and poet famous for Wuthering Heights, not a feminist literary theorist or critic. Virginia Woolf, Simone de Beauvoir, and Judith Butler are foundational figures in feminist and gender theory.

items.title: Q38 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Which of the following is not connected to postmodernism ?
(A) Self-reflexivity
(B) Industrialisation
(C) Magic Realism
(D) Absolutism
(E) Hybridity of Styles
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Postmodernism is characterized by self-reflexivity (A), magic realism (C), and hybridity of styles (E), while rejecting absolutism (D) and the grand narratives of modern industrialisation (B); thus (B) and (D) are not connected to postmodernism.

items.title: Q39 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Deductive method of research intends to
items.explanation: The deductive method of research moves from general principles or theories to particular observations, formulating a hypothesis from a broad theoretical premise and testing it against specific empirical cases.

items.title: Q40 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Rene Descartes
items.stem: Which of the following is not an Empiricist Philosopher ?
items.explanation: Rene Descartes (1596–1650) was the founder of Continental Rationalism, which holds that innate reason rather than sensory experience is the primary source of knowledge, whereas Francis Bacon, John Locke, and David Hume were British Empiricists.

items.title: Q41 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle
items.stem:
Arrange the works of Thomas Carlyle in the chronological order of publication :
(A) Periods of European Culture
(B) Specimens of German Romance
(C) Heroes and Hero Worship
(D) German Literature
(E) Revolution of Modern Europe
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: the chronological sequence of Thomas Carlyle's works is: Specimens of German Romance (B, Jan 1827), 'State of German Literature' (D, Oct 1827), Lectures on the History of Literature / Periods of European Culture (A, 1838), Revolution of Modern Europe (E), and On Heroes, Hero-Worship (C), matching (B), (D), (A), (E), (C).

items.title: Q42 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Hemachandra Joshi, Balwant Gargi, P. K. Bosu, Abdul Ali, D. M. Borgaonkar
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publications :
(A) Hemachandra Joshi's Plays for the Young
(B) Balwant Gargi's The Knife
(C) P. K. Bosu's Conrad and Leonora
(D) Abdul Ali's The Land of Twilight
(E) D. M. Borgaonkar's Image Breakers
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The oldest of these Indian English plays is Abdul Ali's The Land of Twilight, followed by Bosu's Conrad and Leonora, then Gargi's The Knife, Joshi's Plays for the Young and finally Borgaonkar's Image Breakers. (Key doubtful: dates of some titles are hard to confirm.)

items.title: Q43 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary movements in the chronological order :
(A) Feminist Criticism
(B) Deconstruction
(C) Russian Formalism
(D) Phenomenological Criticism
(E) Cultural Studies
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Russian Formalism came first (1910s-20s), then phenomenological criticism (mid-century), feminist criticism, deconstruction and finally Cultural Studies. So the order is C, D, A, B, E.

items.title: Q44 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Choose the correct sequence for writing a research paper :
(A) Gathering Data
(B) Finding a Topic
(C) Finding and Reading the Best Sources
(D) Organizing Ideas and Setting Goals
(E) Writing the Paper
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The logical sequence for writing a research paper begins with Finding a Topic (B), followed by Gathering Data (A), Organizing Ideas and Setting Goals (D), Finding and Reading the Best Sources (C), and finally Writing the Paper (E), corresponding to Option 4: (B), (A), (D), (C), (E).

items.title: Q45 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Nissim Ezekiel
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Hymns in Darkness
(B) The Unfinished Man
(C) A Time to Change and Other Poems
(D) Sixty Poems
(E) The Exact Name
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Nissim Ezekiel's collections appeared as A Time to Change (1952), Sixty Poems (1953), The Unfinished Man (1960), The Exact Name (1965) and Hymns in Darkness (1976). The order is C, D, B, E, A.

items.title: Q46 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Indian English Literature · Unit VI: English in India · Sri Aurobindo, Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publications :
(A) Love and Death
(B) Urvasie : A Poem
(C) Songs to Myrtilla
(D) Savitri
(E) Chitrangada
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Aurobindo's Songs to Myrtilla (1895) and Urvasie (1896) came first, then Tagore's Chitrangada, Love and Death and finally Aurobindo's epic Savitri. So the order is C, B, E, A, D.

items.title: Q47 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Walter Scott, Charlotte Bronte, Elizabeth Gaskell, William Makepeace Thackeray, Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Jane Eyre
(B) Henry Esmond
(C) The Lady of the Last Minstrel
(D) Mary Barton
(E) Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Scott's The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805) came first, then Jane Eyre (1847), Mary Barton (1848), Henry Esmond (1852) and Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1886).

items.title: Q48 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary texts in the order of their publication :
(A) The Taming of the Shrew
(B) Love's Labour Lost
(C) The Merchant of Venice
(D) Much Ado About Nothing
(E) The Winter's Tale
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Shakespeare wrote these roughly in the order Taming of the Shrew (c. 1591), Love's Labour's Lost (c. 1595), Merchant of Venice (c. 1597), Much Ado (c. 1599) and The Winter's Tale (c. 1610).

items.title: Q49 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Orwell, Graham Greene, George Eliot, William Makepeace Thackeray, Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Animal Farm
(B) A Burnt Out Case
(C) The Mill on the Floss
(D) The Book of Snobs
(E) A Tale of Two Cities
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Book of Snobs (1848), A Tale of Two Cities (1859), The Mill on the Floss (1860), Animal Farm (1945), A Burnt Out Case (1961) give the order D, E, C, A, B.

items.title: Q50 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Donne, Edward Herbert, George Herbert, Thomas Carew, James Shirley
items.stem:
What is the correct chronological order of the following poets ?
(A) Thomas Carew
(B) Edward Herbert
(C) John Donne
(D) George Herbert
(E) James Shirley
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Ordered by birth year, the chronological sequence of these seventeenth-century poets is: John Donne (C, 1572), Edward Herbert, Lord Herbert of Cherbury (B, 1583), George Herbert (D, 1593), Thomas Carew (A, 1595), and James Shirley (E, 1596), giving (C), (B), (D), (A), (E).

items.title: Q51 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Augustan Age · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary texts in the order of their publication :
(A) The Dunciad
(B) Essay on Man
(C) The Rape of the Lock
(D) Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot
(E) Windsor Forest
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Pope published The Rape of the Lock (1712), Windsor Forest (1713), The Dunciad (1728), Essay on Man (1733) and Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735). So C, E, A, B, D.

items.title: Q52 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their appearance in the English Literary Scene :
(A) Art for Art's sake
(B) Epistolary Novel
(C) Metaphysical Poetry
(D) Epic Theatre
(E) Stream of Consciousness Technique
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Metaphysical poetry (17th c.) came first, then the epistolary novel (18th c.), Art for Art's sake (19th c.), stream of consciousness (early 20th c.) and epic theatre (1920s-30s).

items.title: Q53 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Walter Pater, Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin, John Richard Green, Charles Darwin
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Studies in the History of the Renaissance by Walter Pater
(B) The French Revolution by Thomas Carlyle
(C) Unto this Last by John Ruskin
(D) The Making of England by John Richard Green
(E) On the Origin of Species by Charles Robert Darwin
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The French Revolution (1837), Origin of Species (1859), Unto this Last (1860), Pater's Studies (1873) and Green's The Making of England (1881) give B, E, C, A, D.

items.title: Q54 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary magazines in the chronological order of their origin or first appearance.
(A) The Westminster Review
(B) The Edinburgh Review
(C) The Quarterly Review
(D) Blackwood's Magazine
(E) The London Magazine
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Edinburgh Review began in 1802, the Quarterly Review in 1809, Blackwood's in 1817, the London Magazine in 1820 and the Westminster Review in 1824.

items.title: Q55 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernism (1900-1945) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Joseph Conrad
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Joseph Conrad in the chronological order of their publication :
(A) Heart of Darkness
(B) Typhoon
(C) Under Western Eyes
(D) The Nigger of the Narcissus
(E) Outcast of the Islands
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Conrad's Outcast of the Islands (1896), The Nigger of the Narcissus (1897), Heart of Darkness (1899), Typhoon (1902) and Under Western Eyes (1911) give E, D, A, B, C.

items.title: Q56 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Sackville, Thomas Norton
items.stem:
The first English tragedy "Gorboduc" was written by :
(A) Nicholas Udall
(B) Thomas Sackville
(C) Thomas Norton
(D) Thomas Lyly
(E) John Heywood
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Gorboduc (also titled Ferrex and Porrex, 1561), the first English blank-verse tragedy, was jointly written by Thomas Norton (who wrote the first three acts) and Thomas Sackville (who wrote the last two acts), corresponding to (B) and (C) Only.

items.title: Q57 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Not period-specific · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Feminist literary and cultural theory draws a link between :
(A) The representation of women in art
(B) Examining how the privileging of some meanings is at the cost of others
(C) The real, material conditions in which women live
(D) The ideological basis of acts of imagination
(E) Providing the native with the means of resistance
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Feminist literary and cultural theory fundamentally links the aesthetic representation of women in art and literature (A) with the real, material, and socio-economic conditions in which women actually live (C), corresponding to (A) and (C) Only.

items.title: Q58 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)

items.explanation: In 'Dover Beach' (1867), Matthew Arnold describes the tranquil English Channel (A), reflects on Sophocles hearing the same 'eternal note of sadness' by the Aegean (C), and laments the retreating 'Sea of Faith' (B), making (A), (B) and (C) Only correct.

items.explanation: Black Feminism focuses on the material realities of Black women's lives (A), critiques patriarchal structures within Black communities and traditions (B), and fosters the solidarity or 'Sisterhood' of Black women (D), corresponding to (A), (B) and (D) Only.

items.title: Q91 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Renaissance · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More
items.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below :
Some have maintained that a stable and tranquil state of health is not really a pleasure, on the grounds that the presence of health cannot be felt except through external stimulus. The Utopians (who have considered the matter thoroughly) long ago rejected this opinion. On the contrary, they nearly all agree that health is crucial to pleasure. Since pain is inherent in diseases, they argue, and pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure, just as disease is the enemy of health, then pleasure must be inherent in quiet good health. You may say pain is not the disease itself, simply an accompanying effect; but they argue that that makes no difference since the effect is the same either way. For whether health is itself a pleasure or is merely the cause of pleasure (as fire is the cause of heat), the fact remains that those who have stable health must also have pleasure.

What does the first line of the passage say about external stimulus ?
options: External stimulus is necessary condition for the experience of health
External stimulus is irrelevant to the experience of health
External stimulus is the by-product of health
items.explanation: The opening line of the passage from Thomas More's Utopia states that the Utopians debate whether health can be felt without some external stimulus, arguing that an external stimulus is a necessary condition for experiencing the sensation of bodily health.

items.title: Q92 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Renaissance · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More
items.stem:

items.explanation: According to the passage, the Utopians hold that tranquil, uninjured bodily health is the foundation and crucial basis of all true pleasure ('Health is crucial to pleasure').

items.title: Q93 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Renaissance · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More
items.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below :
Some have maintained that a stable and tranquil state of health is not really a pleasure, on the grounds that the presence of health cannot be felt except through external stimulus. The Utopians (who have considered the matter thoroughly) long ago rejected this opinion. On the contrary, they nearly all agree that health is crucial to pleasure. Since pain is inherent in diseases, they argue, and pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure, just as disease is the enemy of health, then pleasure must be inherent in quiet good health. You may say pain is not the disease itself, simply an accompanying effect; but they argue that that makes no difference since the effect is the same either way. For whether health is itself a pleasure or is merely the cause of pleasure (as fire is the cause of heat), the fact remains that those who have stable health must also have pleasure.

What according to the Utopians, is the worse enemy of pleasure ?
items.explanation: In the passage, the Utopians explicitly state that 'pain is the bitter enemy of pleasure, just as disease is the enemy of health,' making Pain the worst enemy of pleasure.

items.title: Q96 · Sept 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Post-War & Contemporary · Unit II: Poetry · Seamus Heaney
items.stem:
Read the following passage/poetry carefully and answer the questions given below :
Between my finger and my thumb
The squat pen rests; Snug as a gun.
Under my window, a clean rasping sound:
When the spade sinks into gravelly ground
My father, digging. I look down
Till his straining rump among the flower beds
Bends low, comes up twenty years away
Stooping in rhythm through potato drills
Where he was digging.
The coarse boot nested on the leg, the shaft
Against the inside knee was levered firmly.
He rooted out tall tops, buried the bright edge deep
To scatter new potatoes that we picked,
Loving their cool hardness in our hands.

The comparison of gun to a pen in the poem signifies :
options: the power of written word to bring about change
that the act of writing can be as lethal as using a weapon
the high admiration of the speaker about father's ability to use both pen and spade
items.explanation: In the opening lines of Seamus Heaney's 'Digging' ('Between my finger and my thumb / The squat pen rests; snug as a gun'), the simile comparing the pen to a gun signifies that the act of writing carries a potent, lethal force comparable to a weapon.
